title: Effects of Filipino Consumers' Financial Attitudes, Subjective Norms, and Perceived Behavioral Control on Intentions to Formal Banking: Towards Financial Inclusion
tldr: Social norms and perceived behavioral control significantly predict banking intentions among unbanked Filipinos, while attitudes alone do not, using nationwide survey data and Theory of Planned Behavior framework.
problem_and_motivation: The Philippines has low financial inclusion with only 12.4% of respondents having deposit accounts and 87.6% remaining unbanked as of 2014. Despite BSP's mandate to improve financial access, research on attitudinal and psychological barriers to formal banking remains scarce. This study addresses the gap by examining how attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control influence banking intentions among Filipino consumers using a behavioral lens. The research aims to understand why financial exclusion persists despite observable barriers like cost and lack of funds being addressed.
approach: Utilized the BSP Consumer Financial Survey (CFS) 2014 nationwide quadrennial dataset.
Sample of 15,503 respondents randomly chosen across all Philippine regions.
Applied the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) framework with attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control as primary predictors.
Used logistic regression analysis for the binary dependent variable of banking intention.
Computed chi-square analysis and average marginal effects (AME) using delta method.
Analyzed demographic variables including education, gender, age, income, employment, pension, and household size.
findings: Attitude toward banking was not a significant predictor of intention (β = 0.0186, p = 0.369).
Social norms (having a family member with bank account) significantly predicted intention (β = 0.4397, p = 0.001).
Perceived behavioral control 1 (earning enough to save) significantly predicted intention (β = 0.6158, p = 0.024).
Perceived behavioral control 2 (saving enough for future) negatively predicted intention (β = -0.1098, p = 0.000).
College education significantly increased banking intention compared to no college (β = 0.3344, p = 0.000).
Males were more likely to have banking intention than females (β = 0.0873, p = 0.030).
Baby boomers had lower intention than millennials (β = -0.1202, p = 0.036).
Middle-income individuals had higher intention than low-income (β = 0.1361, p = 0.002).
High-income unbanked individuals had lower intention than low-income (β = -0.4757, p = 0.009).
Unemployed respondents had higher banking intention than employed (β = -0.0818, p = 0.036).
Pension membership significantly increased banking intention (β = 0.3420, p = 0.000).
Household size did not significantly affect intention (β = -0.0108, p = 0.175).
key_figures_tables: Table 1: Response rates across regions - 15,503 respondents, 86.1% response rate.
Table 2: Descriptive statistics - 87.6% unbanked, 12.4% with deposit accounts, 37.4% with deposit intention.
Table 3: Logistic regression results - Model summary with Pseudo R2 = 0.0094, χ2 = 168.65.
Table 4: Marginal effects - AME showing practical significance of each predictor.
key_equations: Logit P(Banking=1) = α + β1X1 + β2X2 + ... + βkXk (logistic regression model)

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This study contributes evidence that social norms and perceived behavioral control, not attitudes alone, drive banking intentions among unbanked Filipinos. The application of Theory of Planned Behavior to Philippine financial inclusion provides a validated behavioral framework. The findings establish that family financial socialization through household members with bank accounts creates 10.16% marginal increase in banking intention. The research demonstrates that demographic factors including education, gender, income, and pension membership significantly predict banking behavior, informing targeted financial inclusion interventions.
directly_justifies: Social norms from family members with bank accounts significantly increase banking intention by 10.16%.
Only 12.4% of Filipinos had deposit accounts in 2014 with 87.6% remaining unbanked.
41.2% of respondents indicated willingness to save in banks if given opportunity.
College education increases banking intention probability by 7.95%.
Pension membership increases banking intention by 8.06%.
limits: Data from 2014 CFS may not reflect current financial behaviors and digital banking adoption.
Focused on deposit account intentions rather than broader investment behaviors.
Cross-sectional design prevents causal inference despite behavioral theory application.
Self-reported data may introduce social desirability bias in financial behavior reporting.
Limited to Philippine context limiting generalizability to other developing economies.
Low pseudo R-squared (0.0094) indicates limited explanatory power of the model.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematic scan across all topic domains identified primary relevance in domains 1 (Filipino professionals and behavior) and 5 (behavioral profiles). Domain 1.A is highly relevant as it profiles Filipino consumers across age, education, income, and employment from nationwide survey. Domain 1.C is highly relevant through examination of banking intentions and financial attitudes. Domain 5.A is moderately relevant for investigating psychological factors shaping behavioral profiles. Domain 5.B is moderately relevant through discussion of loss aversion and risk tolerance. Domains 2-4 (cultural practices, expense categorization, existing systems) were considered but rejected as not directly addressed. Domains 6-8 (forecasting, anomaly detection, mobile design) were considered and rejected as not covered. Domains 9-11 (privacy, engagement, other domains) were considered and rejected as not applicable. Domain 12 (algorithm evaluation) was considered but rejected as the study uses traditional econometric methods rather than algorithmic approaches.
limitations: 2014 data may not capture post-pandemic digital banking transformation in Philippines.
Focus on deposit intentions rather than actual banking behavior or investment patterns.
Low pseudo R-squared suggests other important factors beyond TPB variables influence intention.
Cross-sectional design cannot establish temporal relationships or causal direction.
Self-report methodology may inflate socially desirable financial behaviors.
Single-country focus limits applicability to other developing financial markets.
